newsitem.title: INDIA: India against move in WTO for free investment flow.
newsitem.headline: India against move in WTO for free investment flow.

text.p: India said on Monday it had been joined by several developing countries in opposing a proposal to discuss unrestricted flow of foreign investment at a forthcoming meeting of the World Trade Organisation (WTO).

Commerce Secretary Tejendra Khanna said after a two-day meeting of 14 nations that India also disapproved of a proposal championed by developed nations to make the WTO link environment, labour standards and competition policy to trade.

Indian officials said the meeting did not reach unanimous agreements, but there was a convergence of views on a number of issues in the meeting preparatory to a ministerial meeting of WTO member nations due to be held in Singapore in December.
"We are going to spread the conclusions of this meeting to a large number of developing countries," Khanna told a news conference. "They should stand up and be heard."
Officials from Bangladesh, Brazil, Cuba, Egypt, Ghana, Indonesia, India, Kenya, Malaysia, Mauritius, Tanzania, Thailand, Venezuela and Zimbabwe took part in the meeting.
"It is being argued that having achieved considerable liberalisation of border measures in relation to trade, the next area of liberalisation should cover trans-national investments," said Khanna.
"It was felt by the participants that while investments have a linkage with trade, they also have an important linkage with the development process as a whole," he said in a statement.
"Unless properly regulated to suit the national interests of each country, the impact of trans-national investments can turn out to be more adverse than favourable," the statement said.
India said it also opposed an immediate discussion of competition policies in WTO member nations.

"The meeting agreed that at present many developing countries do not have competition laws and that competition policy is a highly complex subject (that) needs careful study and analysis," the statement said.
Khanna said the meeting expressed concern over persistent efforts to bring labour standards under trade negotiations, reiterating its well-known position in world trade talks.
India, under pressure from western nations to eliminate child labour, says it is committed to the ideal but opposes moves to link trade restrictions with policies on child labour.

The statement also said participants at the meeting felt that developing countries should continue to retain the option of joining a government procurement agreement to ensure free trade rules in state purchases, and not be forced to join it.
The nations that took part in the Delhi meeting also opposed any trade sanctions linked to environmental standards, Khanna said.
"There was a strong objection to unilateral action and disguised protection through trade measures taken for environmental purposes," the statement said.
